content: Neonates often experience immature granulopoiesis, which can lead to neutropenia following sepsis. Neonates with both sepsis and neutropenia have a higher mortality rate compared to those with sepsis but without neutropenia. As a result, granulocyte transfusions have been proposed as a potential intervention to improve outcomes in septic neutropenic neonates. The primary goal of this investigation was to evaluate the impact of granulocyte or buffy coat transfusions, used alongside antibiotics, on all-cause mortality during the hospital stay and on neurological outcomes at or beyond one year of age in neutropenic neonates with confirmed or suspected sepsis. Secondary objectives included assessing the effects of granulocyte transfusions on the length of hospital stay for survivors, adverse effects, and immunological outcomes at or beyond one year of age. A comprehensive search was conducted in July 2011 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, as well as proceedings from the Pediatric Academic Societies (PAS) conferences and ongoing clinical trials registries. Studies were included if they involved neutropenic neonates with suspected or confirmed sepsis who were randomized or quasi-randomized to receive granulocyte or buffy coat transfusions at any dose or duration, and if they reported relevant outcomes. Data analysis involved calculating relative risk (RR) and risk difference (RD) with 95% confidence intervals for dichotomous outcomes using a fixed-effects model. Pre-specified subgroup analyses were also performed. Four trials met the inclusion criteria. Three trials randomized a total of 44 neonates with sepsis and neutropenia to receive either granulocyte transfusions or placebo/no transfusion. A fourth trial randomized 35 neonates with sepsis and neutropenia who were already receiving antibiotics to either granulocyte transfusion or intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). When granulocyte transfusion was compared to placebo or no transfusion, there was no statistically significant difference in all-cause mortality (three trials; typical RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.86; typical RD -0.05, 95% CI -0.31 to 0.21). However, when granulocyte transfusion was compared to IVIG in one trial, there was a borderline statistically significant reduction in all-cause mortality (RR 0.06, 95% CI 0.00 to 1.04; RD -0.34, 95% CI -0.60 to -0.09; number needed to treat [NNT] 2.7, 95% CI 1.6 to 9.1). Pulmonary complications were the only adverse effects reported in trials that utilized buffy coat transfusions. None of the included trials provided data on neurological outcomes at one year of age or later, the length of hospital stay for survivors, or immunological outcomes at one year of age or later. The authors concluded that there is currently insufficient evidence from randomized controlled trials to either support or refute the routine use of granulocyte transfusions in neutropenic, septic neonates. They emphasized the need for adequately powered, multi-center trials to further investigate the efficacy and safety of granulocyte transfusions in this population.
